title: Three Levels of AI Literacy, From Prompts to Agents
summary: Three levels of working with AI: one well-framed request, a workflow you can rerun, and a small agent system with clear limits. Plus when to stay at the simpler level.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Two teammates walk out of the same planning meeting with the same messy notes. One pastes them into a chat window and asks for "a cleaner version." The other drops them into a saved workflow that pulls out decisions, owners, open questions and risks, then drafts the follow-up message and waits for a person to hit send. Same meeting, same kind of tool. By 10 a.m. the second one has done a lot more of the actual work.

That gap is what I mean by AI literacy. Knowing which chat app is popular this month doesn't last, because the apps keep changing. What lasts is framing a problem, splitting the work, giving the model the context it can't guess, and judging whether the output is good enough to move on. This post maps that skill onto three levels, with one working habit for each, plus the signs that tell you to stay at a lower level on purpose.

The core idea

Using AI more often doesn't move you up a level by itself. What moves you up is how much of the work you can design around AI: one better request, a path you can run again, or a small group of agents with clear limits.

Why the bar moved

When generative AI went mainstream, most of us used it as a smarter search box or a fast writing helper. That was useful, and it still is. What changed is that models now call tools and run several steps on their own. Anthropic's engineering team draws a clear line in Building effective agents (December 2024): workflows are systems where "LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths," while agents "dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage." OpenAI's A practical guide to building agents is shorter about it: agents are "systems that independently accomplish tasks on your behalf."

Once a system can act, your job shifts. "What should I ask?" is still a fair question. The heavier ones are: which part of the work should this system do, where should it stop, and how will you know the result is right?

The three levels side by side

The levels describe how you handle one task, so they aren't job titles. You can be at level 1 for emails, level 2 for the weekly report and level 3 for one narrow job you know inside out. The tool names below are examples as of November 2026. Products in this space get renamed, merged and retired often, so read them as categories.

AI OrchestratorWhat small system can carry part of this work?Agent builders (Microsoft Copilot Studio, AI by Zapier (formerly Zapier Agents)), coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor), frameworks (LangGraph)Roles + tools + permissions + checkpoints + metricsAutonomy with no limits and no owner

Level 1: AI Consumer

At this level you use AI one question at a time. Draft an email, tighten a paragraph, summarize a long PDF, explain an error message. The loop is a straight line: ask, read, copy, edit, ask again.

For plenty of tasks that's exactly right. Small chores lose their friction. The weak spot is that everything rides on one prompt and you still do all the stitching. When the answer comes back vague or wrong, the whole flow stalls while you rephrase.

Habit: ask in one complete unit

A request that works usually carries five pieces: the task, the context, the source material, the output format and how you'll judge the result. Compare these two:

  • "Write a LinkedIn post about our launch."
  • "Write a 120-word LinkedIn post for engineering managers about the offline sync feature we just launched. Use only the release notes below. Keep the line about 30-day data retention. No hype words, no emojis. I'll throw it out if it promises dates we haven't announced."

The second one takes a minute longer to write and saves three rounds of "shorter, less salesy, try again." It also spells out how to check the draft, which you'd have to work out anyway.

People at level 1 are often working hard. The catch is that anyone with the same app and the same one-line request gets roughly the same result. You get speed, and no system yet.

Level 2: AI Collaborator

Here you stop treating each request as a one-off and start shaping the work you repeat. A raw call transcript comes out as a structured brief. A customer message comes out as a category, a draft reply and a risk flag. A messy export comes out as a clean table and a short summary, in the same shape every week.

A few jobs that fit this level well:

  • Meeting notes: transcript in; decisions, open questions, owners and draft tickets for Jira or Linear out. You read them before any ticket gets created.
  • Writing: voice notes in, grouped into themes, one angle picked by you, then an outline, a draft and a final pass that checks claims and tone.
  • Sales follow-up: call notes in, objections pulled out, one CRM field updated, a follow-up email drafted and held until someone approves it.

Habit: make the path rerunnable

The habit at this level is a five-step chain:

  1. Input: decide what raw material goes in and where it comes from.
  2. Normalize: get it into a stable shape (same headings, same fields, same date format).
  3. Transform: produce the useful output.
  4. Review: check it before it leaves your desk.
  5. Handoff: send it to the next place, whether that's a doc, a ticket, a CRM or a person.

In Anthropic's terms this is a workflow: the steps are fixed ahead of time and the model fills in each one. That's a strength. Fixed steps are easy to test, cheap to run and easy to debug when something breaks. Both Anthropic and OpenAI tell builders to start with setups like this. OpenAI's guide says that unless the job really needs judgment over messy, unstructured input, "a deterministic solution may suffice."

A quick test

Run the same AI-assisted process three times on similar inputs. If the output comes back in a shape you could have predicted, you have a workflow. If every run surprises you, look at step 2 first: the input usually isn't normalized yet.

You also get better at debugging here. When an output is weak, you check which step broke (bad input, missing context, a vague format) before you blame the model. You stop expecting the first answer to be the last one.

Level 3: AI Orchestrator

At level 3 you design the system that runs the steps, and you stop running them by hand. You start from the goal and split it into roles. One agent gathers sources. Another compares them. Another drafts. Another flags unsupported claims, risk or tone problems. You're still in the loop, in a different seat: you set the direction, define what "good" means, decide what each role may touch and put checks around the parts that must not fail.

The tools depend on who you are. An operations lead might use an agent builder like Microsoft Copilot Studio or AI by Zapier (formerly Zapier Agents). A software team might use a coding agent like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, or build on a framework like LangGraph (all examples as of November 2026). The names will shift again next year. The pattern stays: give each role the tools it needs and nothing more, limit what it can write or send, and mark the spots where a human decides.

Some concrete shapes:

  • Product: one agent summarizes the week's support tickets, one groups them into pain points, one links those to roadmap items, and a person reads the brief before it goes to leadership.
  • Content: a research agent collects source notes, a writing agent drafts, an editor agent flags claims with no source and ideas that repeat.
  • Hiring: separate flows for screening, interview questions and candidate emails, with a person approving every message that leaves the company.

If you want the mechanics of how agents plan and call tools, AI agents explained goes deeper.

Habit: write down the operating model

The habit here is an operating model, written down before the first run:

  • Who owns the goal and the final result?
  • Which agents can only read data, and which can write or send?
  • Where does the system stop and ask a person?
  • Which actions can be undone, and which can't?
  • Which numbers tell you it's helping, as opposed to creating cleanup work?

These questions are less fun than the demo. They're also where the reliability comes from.

People sometimes call this a "boss mindset." The part worth keeping is responsibility. A good manager doesn't hand out tasks and hope for the best. They make the goal clear, give enough context, pick the right person for each job, check the points that matter and own the outcome. Directing agents asks for the same posture.

Guardrails are the actual skill

You don't need to become a software engineer to work at level 2 or 3. You do need to think about the work more clearly. What's the real goal? Which parts repeat? Which parts need judgment? What data is safe to hand over? Where should the AI stop and ask?

OpenAI's guide names two moments to hand control back to a person: the agent keeps failing past a limit you set (retries, attempts), or it's about to do something sensitive, irreversible or high-stakes, like canceling an order, approving a large refund or making a payment. That's a solid starting list. Anthropic adds stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations, and recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments, with guardrails in place.

Then there's checking the output. The smoother AI writing gets, the easier it is to treat a polished answer as finished work, and your gut is a poor meter here. In METR's early-2025 study, 16 experienced open-source developers took 19% longer on real issues when they were allowed AI tools, yet afterward they estimated AI had sped them up by 20%. METR's February 2026 update says developers are likely sped up more by newer tools, and also that its new data is skewed by who agreed to take part, so it can't give a reliable number yet. The tools have moved on. The gap between how fast work feels and how fast it is still deserves a measurement. For a practical rule on when an answer needs checking, see When an AI answer needs a test.

The failure mode to avoid

The risky way to adopt AI is giving a system autonomy before anyone has written down its scope, permissions, review points and owner. Picking the wrong tool hurts far less. A fast workflow with no owner just ships mistakes faster.

Climb only when the task asks for it

A ladder makes it sound like the top is the goal. It isn't, and the people who build agents for a living say so plainly. Anthropic warns that agents bring "higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors," and suggests adding complexity only when it clearly improves the result. OpenAI's guide advises getting the most out of a single agent before splitting work across several.

So before moving a task up a level, check which situation you're in:

  • Stay at level 1 when the task is a one-off, or when you'd read every word of the output anyway.
  • Move to level 2 when you've done the task three or more times and the steps barely change.
  • Consider level 3 only when the steps can't be fixed in advance, the input is messy and unstructured, and you can measure whether the agent actually did better than your workflow.

Most of your work will sit at level 1 or 2, and that's a good outcome. For ideas on which repeated tasks to pick first, AI workflows that save hours has a list.

Try this week

  • Pick one task you did at least three times last month.
  • Write the five-piece request for it (task, context, source, format, how you'll judge it) and save it where you'll find it again.
  • Run it on three real inputs. If the outputs come back in different shapes, fix the input format before you touch the prompt.
  • For each step, write one line: who reviews it, and what would make them reject it.
  • Only if the steps truly can't be fixed in advance, try a single agent with read-only tools, a retry limit and a human approval before anything gets sent.

AI keeps pushing you to describe goals precisely, split work carefully and say what "good" looks like. Those habits make your work better with or without a model in the loop, so they're worth practicing on purpose.

faqs.q: What does AI literacy mean once agents are involved?
faqs.a: It's the ability to frame a task clearly, give the model the context it can't guess, judge whether the output is good enough, and, with agents, decide what a system may do on its own and where it has to stop and ask a person. Knowing a particular app matters much less, because the apps change every year.

faqs.q: Which tools fit each level of AI literacy?
faqs.a: As of November 2026: level 1 is a chat assistant such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or NotebookLM. Level 2 adds saved projects and automation tools such as Zapier, Make or n8n. Level 3 uses agent builders such as Microsoft Copilot Studio or AI by Zapier (formerly Zapier Agents), coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, or frameworks such as LangGraph. Names change often, so treat them as categories.

faqs.q: What does a good AI workflow look like?
faqs.a: Five steps that run the same way every time: input (what goes in and from where), normalize (a stable shape), transform (the useful output), review (a person checks it) and handoff (it goes to a doc, ticket, CRM or person). If three runs on similar inputs give outputs in a shape you could predict, the workflow is working.

faqs.q: Do non-technical people need to learn to code to use AI well?
faqs.a: No. Clear thinking matters more: naming the goal, describing constraints, splitting work into steps, spotting where judgment is needed and checking whether the output is reliable enough to use. Code helps at level 3 if you build agents yourself, but agent builders cover a lot without it.

faqs.q: When should an AI agent hand control back to a person?
faqs.a: OpenAI's agent guide names two triggers: the agent fails past a limit you set, such as a number of retries, or it's about to take an action that is sensitive, irreversible or high-stakes, like canceling an order, approving a large refund or making a payment. Anthropic also recommends stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations.

faqs.q: Should every task move up to agents?
faqs.a: No. Anthropic and OpenAI both advise starting with the simplest setup that works and adding agents only when the result clearly improves. Fixed workflows are cheaper, easier to test and easier to debug. Agents fit open-ended tasks where the steps can't be decided in advance.
